title: Chefs Charlie Palmer, Liza Gershman Celebrate Sonoma County Food in New Cookbooks
summary:
The new locally produced cookbooks, both with Healdsburg roots, feature chefs, farmers and artisans producing the best of Wine Country food.

The post Chefs Charlie Palmer, Liza Gershman Celebrate Sonoma County Food in New Cookbooks appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The summer bounty is officially here and with it come two new, locally produced cookbooks, both with Healdsburg roots, that celebrate the very best of local food.

James Beard Award-winning chef Charlie Palmer’s “Wineland,” penned with Healdsburg journalist Matt Villano, features 20 Wine Country culinary luminaries from Sonoma, Napa, and Marin Counties who share their life stories and favorite recipes.

“The way we live here is an ideal, a philosophy, built around hard work and relationships,” says Palmer, a Healdsburg resident who chased that dream when relocating from New York with his family 25 years ago. “We make and grow and build and create. Community is paramount — this is about the most real place you can get.”

Some of the storytelling also comes from work of local photographer Emma Kruch, who spent more than a year trekking from cloud-blanketed mountaintops to being hip-deep in brackish bay waters to capture more than 125 images that add to the book’s artistry.

Flipping through the glossy pages, you can practically taste Liam Callahan’s tangy-sweet sheep’s milk cheese dotted with herbs from Bellwether Farms in Petaluma and smell the briny air at John Finger and Terry Sawyer’s Hog Island Oyster Co. on Tomales Bay.

The Healdsburg Farmers Market is the setting for Sonoma County native Liza Gershman’s latest cookbook, “Farm + Market: Healdsburg,” which reads like a love letter to the community that revolves in and around the beloved market.

Founded in 1978, the Healdsburg Farmers Market is one of the oldest certified markets in California. Gershman, who has written and photographed 20 cookbooks, celebrates the local farmers, ranchers, makers, chefs, and even home cooks who are the heart and soul of the market that runs Saturdays, April through December, and Tuesdays, May through September. A portion of proceeds from the book goes right back into the market to ensure it continues to thrive.

Rebecca Richards is one of its champions; she fell in love with Healdsburg 15 years ago and convinced her husband they needed to move from San Francisco. After visiting the market, she quickly got swept in with the community, and before she knew it, was on the board and helping with bookkeeping.

“I’m very into recipes and going to the market to see what’s in season,” says Richards, whose recipe for an arugula, nectarine, and quinoa salad demonstrates her respect for seasonal ingredients and the farmers who nurture them. Local nectarines are at their finest in June through August.

“I think people just assume that you can get anything at any time, which you kind of can, but that doesn’t mean it’s at its peak,” she says. “It kills me when I go to a restaurant in January and they’re serving BLTs. And I’m like, ‘No!’ I have to wait for summer for a real, happy tomato.”

A Tale of Two Cookbooks

Wineland is best for:

  • Friends and family who love to visit Wine Country
  • Those who want the story behind their favorite restaurants, wineries, and producers
  • Accomplished home cooks

Find it at local bookstores and at charliepalmer.com.

Farm + Market is ideal for: 

  • Farmers Market aficionados
  • Collectors of community cookbooks
  • Local history buffs

Find it at healdsburgbook.com.

title: Sarmentine Bakery in Petaluma Is the Spot for Crepe Cravings
summary:
The baker at this favorite Sonoma County boulangerie trained at a French school devoted entirely to traditional Breton crepes.

The post Sarmentine Bakery in Petaluma Is the Spot for Crepe Cravings appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Perfected along the coast of Brittany more than 1,500 years ago, crepes are serious business in France. There’s even a holiday dedicated to them where their golden, sun-like shape is tied to luck, prosperity, and tradition as much as it is to breakfast or lunch.

At Petaluma’s Sarmentine bakery, Alexandra Teulet has introduced diners to the art of the crepe, making both sweet varieties and a savory buckwheat version called a galette, a specialty of France’s northwestern coast. She trained in Saint-Malo at a school devoted entirely to traditional Breton crepes — yes, really.

Making them well is part instinct, part technique: the feel of the lightly fermented batter, the grind of the nutty buckwheat flour, and the steady heat of a traditional cast-iron billig crepe maker.

The crepes emerge thin with delicately lacy edges that fold and frame fillings like bubbling cheese, ham, vegetables, fruit, or chocolate. Teulet turns out several hundred a day, exclusively at the Petaluma location, bringing a true taste of Brittany to Sonoma County.

840 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma. 707-623-9595, sarmentine.com

title: Celebrate Local Author Jack London’s 150th Birthday in the Valley of the Moon
summary:
Famed author Jack London's legacy is felt all over, especially in Sonoma Valley. His namesake Glen Ellen park is celebrating his 150th birthday all year long with special events.

The post Celebrate Local Author Jack London’s 150th Birthday in the Valley of the Moon appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Author Jack London’s legacy is felt far and wide, but especially in Glen Ellen where he built his dream ranch, now home to Jack London State Historic Park, which is celebrating his 150th birthday all year long with special events.

Here’s a look at London and his namesake park in Glen Ellen, by the numbers.

93,350 visitors to Jack London State Historic Park in 2025.

8 varieties of fruit trees in the park’s historic orchard, some of which are more than 100 years old.

4,029 books sold at the bookstore in the House of Happy Walls Museum last year. 70% of those were books by Jack London.

2,370 feet is the highest elevation in the park at the end of the Mountain Spur Trail. It offers views of Sonoma Valley and as far as Mount Diablo, some 45 miles away as the crow flies.

15,200 hours logged last year by 250 park volunteers who do everything from leading tours and hikes to playing the 125-year-old Steinway grand piano in the museum.

3,000 pounds of fruit donated from the historic orchard to Farm to Pantry in 2025.

2,200+ acres of land makes up Jack London State Historic Park, which grew in recent years when 650 acres of open space land from the Sonoma Developmental Center was transferred to California State Parks.

51 tours and programs provided for 24 schools last year.

167,551 words in London’s book, “Valley of the Moon,” his longest. The novel follows the journey of a working-class couple who leave the city in a search for farmland.

750 dollars is how much London made when he sold “The Call of the Wild” to The Saturday Evening Post in 1903. That equates to roughly $27,000 today.

37 entries in the 2026 Young Writers Contest put on by Jack London Park for middle school students. This is the contest’s 11th year.

Jack London Park Partners Gala

Jack’s 150th: A Bold Wish, from 5-9 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026

Enjoy a night of food, wine, and music in the Eucalyptus Grove and among the winery ruins with dinner from Park Avenue Catering and wines provided by Lasseter Family Winery. Tickets: $350. 2400 London Ranch Road, Glen Ellen. 707-938-5216, jacklondonpark.com

title: Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation
summary:
A rugged Monte Rio refuge quadrupled in size last year, offering nearly 30 miles of trails lovingly maintained by an all-volunteer local cycling association.

The post Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
If you favor fat-tire biking and seek epic singletrack through postcard stands of Sequoia, head for Monte Rio Redwoods Park and Open Space Preserve. That rugged west county refuge quadrupled in size a year ago when Sonoma County Regional Parks acquired, from Save the Redwoods League, a 1,517-acre parcel laced with nearly 30 miles of trails. It was built and maintained for decades by members of the Gianni Cycling Association, named for the beloved Occidental bike shop that closed its doors in 1998.

Save the Redwoods League bought that timberland in 2025 from the Mendocino Redwood Company, which had allowed Gianni’s members to build trails and ride their bikes on the property.

Through the years, the cycling association, an all-volunteer nonprofit, has been the beating heart of mountain biking in west Sonoma County, earning a reputation for its superb stewardship of the land and the high quality of its trails. The steep singletracks — narrow, natural surface paths — and fast flow sections are designed to maximize fun while minimizing impact on the environment.

Tom “Snap” Gonnella, who owned Gianni’s Cyclery and founded the club named after it, recalled in a recent podcast, “We were trying to be as inclusive as we could, but we had to deal with the landlord, who was limiting us on how many bikes that we could have in there.”

Now in the hands of Regional Parks, the cap on users is lifted. “We get to share it with everyone,” says Jake Bayless, a Gianni member who notes that, due to the park’s relative remoteness, fears of overcrowding have faded. “Everybody loves seeing more people riding bikes and smiling,” he says. “It’s a magic place.”

Learn more about becoming a volunteer member of the Gianni Cycling Association at giannicycling.org.

Riding the Redwoods

Most of the park’s trails fall in the intermediate category. An introductory route is the 2.3-mile Monte Rio Redwoods Trail, a lollipop loop through towering redwoods, along singletrack and old logging roads, featuring 600 feet of climbing, which even the fittest riders may find challenging.

A far more ambitious undertaking is the 6.8-mile Radar Love Loop, which calls for 1,765 feet of climbing and offers sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean at the halfway point.

Access trails via the park’s main entrance, 9610 Main St. in Monte Rio, or from the trailhead at 25572 Freezeout Road with a parking lot managed by California State Parks.

The Upper Willow Creek Road trailhead, offering access to a plethora of scenic routes — Badfinger, Sound of Music, Eastside and East Ramps loop, to name a few — has very limited parking along Willow Creek Road. Many bikers ride from Occidental, 5 miles away.

After riding the bikes-only Vacation Wonderland Trail at Monte Rio Redwoods, stop in at the newly opened Wonderland Pizzeria for a pie and a pint on their expansive patio. 20391 Highway 116, Monte Rio. 707-865-5133, instagram.com/wonderland_pizzeria

This article was excerpted from our Ultimate Guide to Sonoma County’s Great Outdoors, originally published in the July/August 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer
summary:
Italian white wine varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The post These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When it comes to crisp white wines, Sauvignon Blanc isn’t the only game in town. Italian white varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The delicious proof was on full display at this year’s North Coast Wine Challenge. Competing in the sweepstakes round for top honors were two Sonoma County Italians: a Fiano from DaVero Farms & Winery and a Biancolella d’Ischia from Orsi Family Vineyards.

The trend comes as no surprise to local winemakers like Sam Bilbro. He’s the founder and winemaker at Idlewild Wines in Healdsburg, which specializes in Italian-inspired wines.

“Italian varietals offer such a diversity of flavor profiles and joyful food friendliness,” says Bilbro, who makes wine from a Piedmontese grape called Erbaluce, planted at Las Cimas Ranch on the western edge of Russian River Valley.

“One of the qualities I love about this grape is that it has extreme fresh acidity matched with a textural mouthfeel,” he says. “I find that the aromatics are more driven by mineral tones and fresh Alpine scents with an undertone of orchard fruit.”

Eric Prahl, winemaker at Centennial Mountain Winery in Healdsburg, believes Sonoma County is an especially hospitable place for Italian whites. The Centennial Mountain vineyard includes California’s only planting of Carricante, hailing from Sicily.

“Italian varieties like Carricante have evolved over centuries to maintain balance in warm climates, which makes them highly relevant for the future of Sonoma County,” he says. “They offer a texture and a savory, saline quality that is still relatively uncommon here.”

Bilbro points out that Italian whites grown here sometimes express themselves a little differently in the glass.

“If made in a restrained style,” he says, “I find that Sonoma County is very true to the core of the varietals, as well as showing perhaps just a touch of California sunshine in the fruit tone.”

Three to try

Idlewild Wines

2023 Erbaluce, Las Cimas Vineyard, Russian River Valley, $42

With a vibrant golden color, Idlewild’s Erbaluce combines notes of lemon, fresh herbs and bright acidity. Made without oak, it’s fresh, juicy and food-friendly. 132 Plaza St., Healdsburg, 707-385-9410, idlewildwines.com

Orsi Family Vineyards

2024 Biancolella d’Ischia, Dry Creek Valley, $28

Made from a grape traditionally grown on the island of Ischia, Biancolella is known for its crispness, light body and subtle almond finish. Orsi’s is true to type — a mineral-kissed wine with tropical fruit aromas. 2306 Magnolia Drive, Healdsburg, 707-732-4660, orsifamilyvineyards.com

Centennial Mountain

2022 Carricante, Sonoma County , $49

With a lightly floral aroma, this energetic white shows off notes of citrus, minerals and fresh herbs. Intense, yet full of freshness and zing. It is delicious now, but you could also lay it down for a couple years to see how it develops. 337 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 669-240-5611, cmvineyard.com

title: Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub
summary:
Here are some Sonoma County gas stations with food options that may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

The post Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
It’s summertime, which means road trips and hungry travelers clamoring for quick eats. Sure, there are drive-ins, but there are some unexpected surprises at full service fuel shops where you can fill up your car and your belly. We’re not talking about sad hot dogs spinning on roller grills.

Here are some Sonoma County gas stations whose food options may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

Wine Country Café & Deli

Stop in at the Fast Fill Market and Gulf station and treat yourself to the marvelous from-scratch scones, organic apple hand pies, all-day breakfast (smoked salmon croissant!) and plump, made-to-order sandwiches (legit banh mi and coffee-rubbed barbecue tri-tip). Spring through autumn finds barbecue, smashburgers, or street taco pop-ups every Friday in the parking lot. 5855 Sonoma Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-230-2462, winecountrycafedeli.toast.site

Husary 76

Its website lists it as a “convenience store,” but besides diesel and propane, you’ll discover gourmet grub such as real-deal Mexican hot chocolate, and — get this — a countertop wine fridge filled with olive oil crafted from a grove of trees nearby. Station owner and lifelong Sonoma County resident Mousa Husary looked to his Palestinian roots for planting his orchards and producing award-winning extra-virgin cold-pressed olive oil. 2110 Gravenstein Highway N., Sebastopol. 707-829-8252, husaryoliveoil.com

Bonneau Country

A gas station that has its own website with a category titled “cuisine”? This is Wine Country, after all. Find snacks and an early-morning drive-thru barista window at the station’s northern outpost at Arnold Drive and Grove Street. Five miles south at the roundabout, where Highway 116 meets Highway 121, the Carneros Deli just across the parking lot from the fueling and electric charging stations is the place for made-to-order delights: hot and cold sandwiches built from fancy stuff like premium prosciutto, provolone, all the fixings, and an array of breads and spreads including the must-have “spicy boom boom” sauce. 19080 Arnold Drive and 23001 Arnold Drive, Sonoma. 707-939-1646, bonneaucountry.com

Fuel & Food Market

The calling card is the Krispy Krunchy Chicken sign, beckoning you in for the cult-favorite hand-battered bird, the real discovery, though, is the under-the-radar Indian market filled with pantry staples like lentils, rice, and spices ranging from cardamom to black mustard seed. Even the frozen food is a step-up from ordinary, including naan, samosas and kulfi, an Indian specialty similar to ice cream. 4856 Old Redwood Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-843-4083

Vinoma Tapas Argentina

It’s not technically within a gas station, yet beckons from the adjacent Shell parking lot a few steps away. And you would be hard-pressed to find better fast-casual empanadas. These golden-brown Argentinian treats are stuffed with goodness like traditional spiced beef, a vegan curry tofu, or specialties like the plum, bacon, fontina and mozzarella open-faced version called canastita. 5085 Redwood Drive, Rohnert Park. 707-536-9215, vinoma.net

title: Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria
summary:
Carrusel owner Ivy Reyes has transformed a childhood dream into an over-the-top Santa Rosa bruncheria filled with pink velvet, carousel horses and playful Mexi-brunch dishes.

The post Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Santa Rosa’s newest — and pinkest — brunch spot began with Ivy Reyes’ childhood dream of owning an Easy-Bake Oven.

Though her family couldn’t afford one, Reyes never forgot the toy oven or her dream of opening a bakery. Decades later, she opened Carrusel, a portal to her youth and a fantasyland of glitter, bows, flowers and carousel horses that makes Barbie’s Dreamhouse look restrained.

“My childhood is poured into here,” Reyes said.

Dressed head to toe in sparkles and sipping a pink Red Bull at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday (what else would she drink?), Reyes radiates Barbie glamour. At 33, the Instagram influencer, who drives a pink Range Rover and dreams up elaborate social media promotions, is very much queen of all she surveys.

“This is just me,” she said, wrapping manicured pink nails around the heart-shaped straw in her energy drink. “I put it together for the love of food, color and a dream. I want it to be an enchantment.”

These days, Reyes is no longer dreaming about an Easy-Bake Oven. She’s overseeing a staff of 50, an ambitious cocktail program and a six-page Mexi-brunch menu that keeps the kitchen busy.

Family roots

Beneath the spectacle is a family story built on work and sacrifice.

Reyes, her immigrant parents and two brothers shared a one-bedroom apartment while the family built La Fondita restaurant and Elenita’s food truck in Roseland. She grew up alongside her mother in the kitchen, learning both the food and business sides of the restaurant industry.

“Growing up, it was very, very worrisome when my parents were starting out and living check to check,” she said. “I remember that, and it keeps me humble.”

Her mother eventually gave Reyes the opportunity to build something of her own, transforming the former La Fondita downtown into something entirely new.

“She put everything on a silver platter,” Reyes said. “From there, she said, ‘Fly with it. You’re on your own.’”

Reyes had hoped her grandmother would be the first person through Carrusel’s doors. Before she died, Reyes showed her the nearly finished restaurant by phone from the hospital and received her blessing.

“I’ve had people of all ages tear up here,” Reyes said. “It brings out the inner child in everyone.”

Flowers, candles and bright colors had always lifted her spirits, and she wanted Carrusel to offer guests the same escape.

“When your world goes gray, paint it pink,” she said. “You can have a bad day, come in here and forget the problems you’re having.”

Best bets

Carrusel is about fun and fantasy rather than fine dining. Expect cotton-candy-topped cocktails, tacos served on a high wire and a Mexi-brunch menu that blends American and Latin flavors with carnival flair. Desserts lean unapologetically sweet, with glazes, marshmallows and chocolate piled high.

And yes, you can eat on the outdoor carousel, which somehow makes everything taste more fun.

Raspberry Mocha Truffle, $8: The fact that I’ve ordered this three times says plenty about my weakness for sugar, glitter and caffeine. Thick raspberry foam (banana and blueberry are also available), edible butterflies (I use “edible” loosely) and chocolatey iced mocha make this a memorable way to start the day. Or night.

Queso Birria Tacos, $20: One of the menu’s most entertaining presentations, with three consommé-soaked birria tacos suspended on a clothesline-like rack. Fiery avocado salsa and extra consommé for dipping complete the show.

Enmoladas, $20: Not the prettiest dish on the menu, but one of the most satisfying. Rich, dark mole blankets chicken-filled tortillas. Sometimes no glitter is needed.

Brunch Board, $35: Order this butterfly-shaped board simply because you can. It comes loaded with banana French toast, strawberry-topped pancakes, a berry-topped Belgian waffle, fresh fruit and Nutella.

Funnel Cake, $18: This fairground favorite is available year-round, piled high with fruit, powdered sugar, chocolate and bananas whenever the craving strikes.

Japanese Pancakes, $18: These take about 20 minutes to make and involve a special technique known only to the kitchen. They aren’t quite as airy as the versions popularized in Japan, but they’re close enough.

Cloud Nine, $18: Dragon berry rum, lychee, lemon and vanilla topped with a cloud of cotton candy — exactly what your 9-year-old self imagined you would be drinking at 21.

Mimosa Flight, $38: Every mimosa should come this way. More brunchy fun for everyone.

Chilaquiles, $19: Judging by the number landing on neighboring tables, this may be the restaurant’s most popular dish.

Open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily. Carrusel is at 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel.

title: Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around
summary:
Yvette Bidegain carries on her father’s barbecue legacy with catfish, ribs, fried chicken and plenty of personality at Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint.

The post Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Yvette Bidegain thought she knew what Californians wanted to eat. Okra and catfish weren’t on the list.

Four years after opening Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville, they’re her two best-selling dishes.

“I used to sneak catfish to my friends’ table because they really wanted it,” she said. Other diners noticed and started asking for it, too. Eventually, the farm-raised catfish earned a permanent place on the menu.

Saucy Mama’s is equal parts soul food restaurant, neighborhood hangout, birthday destination and post-river stop, wrapped in a barbecue-roadhouse-meets-New Orleans aesthetic.

Tucked along a bend in Highway 116 west of downtown Guerneville, it’s the kind of place many drivers pass on their way to the coast. Yet Saucy Mama’s is almost always full, with Bidegain greeting guests and keeping the dining room humming. Some regulars even plan vacations around getting a “Saucy Mama fix.”

Bidegain’s menu blends the Southern cooking of her family’s Louisiana and Mississippi roots with her own California sensibility. Since opening in 2022, the restaurant has built a loyal following.

The backstory

Bidegain is the daughter of Leroy Richardson, whose Richardson’s Ribs was a Sonoma County Fair favorite in the 1980s and ’90s before expanding into restaurants in Santa Rosa and Sebastopol. His recipes remain the backbone of Saucy Mama’s menu.

At first, Bidegain resisted leaning on the family name.

“I didn’t want to take my dad’s name down with me,” she said.

Then her mother tasted Bidegain’s gumbo and delivered the compliment that mattered most: “Baby, your gumbo tastes just like your daddy’s.”

She knew she was onto something.

Richardson’s recipes live on in Bidegain’s kitchen, while signs, menus, family photographs and other mementos from his restaurants cover the walls.

Not every dish would have earned her father’s approval. Bidegain jokes he’s probably rolling over in his grave over the tofu po’ boy and meatless succotash.

Even the restaurant’s bright red smoker felt like fate. Bidegain had gone to a restaurant supply store looking for a sink and instead found a used Texas smoker she’d long pined for — marked down to half price.

“A lot of things happened like that for us,” she said. “I truly think my father was orchestrating it from heaven.”

Here’s what to know before you go.

Yvette’s favorite dish

Pork ribs.

Fun fact

Bidegain didn’t like soul food growing up. While her friends ate spaghetti with Parmesan, she dreaded collard greens, neck bones and black-eyed peas.

That changed in her 20s, when she started cooking for herself. During her pregnancy, she found herself craving the dishes she’d once avoided.

“It’s just in my DNA,” she said. “Your blood takes over.”

The vibe

You will not get in without a reservation, so don’t try to sweet-talk Bidegain, who is usually at the front door greeting guests. When the restaurant is full, it’s full.

The crowd ranges from birthday celebrants in dress clothes to river-goers in flip-flops, and nobody looks out of place.

Inside, Saucy Mama’s is a joyful jumble of vintage New Orleans signs, memorabilia from Richardson’s restaurants, Black art and hundreds of donated knickknacks. Maximalist hardly begins to describe it.

Every holiday brings another round of decorations. “Restraint” is not in her vocabulary. Bidegain originally envisioned a true jook joint with live music and dancing, but the restaurant became so popular there’s barely room between the tables.

The food

Come hungry. Portions are generous, and nobody comes here to count calories.

Crispy fried catfish entree, $20: The seasoned cornmeal crust is crisp and flavorful, without the heavy, bready coating that can sink lesser catfish. Inside, the farm-raised fish is moist, succulent and clean-tasting.

Shrimp po’ boy, $22: A small French loaf is cut into a boat rather than sliced through, holding a messy pile of fried shrimp, lettuce, tomatoes and remoulade.

Buttermilk fried chicken entree, $25: The boldly seasoned crust fries up crisp, giving way to juicy meat. Pair it with red beans and rice and collard greens for the soul food holy trinity. The loose bits of crunchy crust left on the plate are worth chasing with a fork. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Barbecue pork ribs entree, $28: Coated in Bidegain’s secret dry rub for at least 24 hours before spending hours in the smoker, the ribs are deeply smoky and tender. They’re slathered in a sweet barbecue sauce and best eaten with plenty of napkins. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Extras, $8: Great barbecue restaurants live or die by their sides. Here, the macaroni and cheese — made with four cheeses and cream — is rich and satisfying. The standout, though, is the fried okra tossed with onions and bacon.

All meats are available à la carte, including a full rack of pork ribs and fried chicken.

Banana pudding, $6: Even banana pudding skeptics may be won over by this version, layered into a shortbread crust and topped with whipped cream.

The menu also includes several gluten-free and vegetarian options, along with beer, cider, wine and nonalcoholic drinks.

The discount

Because Bidegain spent years as a Caltrans equipment operator, she offers a 10% discount to fellow operating engineers.

The spot

16632 Highway 116, Guerneville, 707-604-7184, saucymamasjookjoint.com

title: Bay Area Designer’s Cape Dutch-Style Home Hits the Market in Glen Ellen
summary:
The Glen Ellen home references traditional architecture from South Africa’s acclaimed wine region and includes whimsical touches like cast-iron street lamps and a British phone booth.

The post Bay Area Designer’s Cape Dutch-Style Home Hits the Market in Glen Ellen appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Glen Ellen home with Cape Dutch style is currently listed for sale. The farmhouse, guest house, barn-style office and pool on 16 acres is currently seeking $12,000,000.

The home is the work of resident and designer Patrick Printy — a veteran style-maker for major brands, such as Levi’s and Restoration Hardware, and lead of his own firm with projects published in magazines from Elle Decor to House Beautiful. 

This particular three-bedroom, three-bathroom farmhouse references traditional architecture from South Africa’s wine country. A unique design for the Sonoma area, the dwelling has the signature Cape Dutch scalloped, ornamented gables. Inside, there’s handcrafted Dutch cabinetry by Johannes Van Mourik and also handmade Dutch “witjes” tiles.

Use of grandly sized oak wood beams and floor planks, reclaimed from Midwestern barns, creates dramatic farm character throughout. The property’s exterior stonework was sourced from rocks quarried from the property.

Eclectic textiles create a cohesive but collected look. The interiors are an impossibly successful mix of old and new, clean-lined and traditional with pleasing dollops of fun tossed in. This is exemplified right at the front door where black-and-white traditional symmetry is made playful with the addition of wonderfully “matchy” Dalmatian statues. Vintage cast-iron street lamps, sourced from San Francisco’s China Basin, and a British phone booth offer spectacular whimsy to the grounds.

The grounds include a pond, a well and solar panels. There are two additional parcels for future development.

For more information on this Glen Ellen property, contact listing agent Tina Shone, 707-799-7556, 707-933-1515; Sotheby’s International Realty – Wine Country – Sonoma Brokerage, 793 Broadway, Sonoma, sothebysrealty.com/eng/sales/detail/180-l-1188-4gm75q/artfully-crafted-beautifully-appointed-glen-ellen-ca-95442

title: Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale
summary:
Boasting over 38,000 lavender plants, Monte-Bellaria has long drawn visitors with its rich sensory experience and handmade lavender products. Now the farm and hilltop home is on the market.

The post Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Sebastopol estate with a lavender farm — one of the largest in northern California — is currently listed for sale. A four-bedroom, three-and-half-bathroom home on 14 acres with 38,000 lavender plants, an olive orchard, apiary and farm store are listed for $4,995,000.

The property, named Monte-Bellaria — meaning “mountain of beautiful air” in Italian — has been a beloved stop along the Sonoma County Farm Trails. The land, stewarded since 2002 by the late Dr. Bill MacElroy, has sloping rows of the hardy and fragrant Grosso lavender plant.

Yearly, MacElroy, along with farm manager and beekeeper Eric Silas, cultivated and harvested the lavender, from which he would distill the essential oils to create the property’s popular products: soaps, balms, hydrosols and a sumptuous lavender honey. The handmade goods, including olive oils made from the yields of their orchard, were sold at the on-site farm store. Monte-Bellaria became a popular site for visitors seeking tranquility, a bit of shopping and a swoon-worthy photo backdrop.

A walk through the grounds is a rich sensory experience. In addition to the immense fragrance during high bloom season, there’s a sound bath of buzzing from the bees hard at work pollinating the plants. 

The 4,965-square-foot hilltop home, built in 2014, takes style cues from the Tuscan countryside, which inspired MacElroy’s development of the farm. The dwelling is airy with high ceilings, lime-washed walls in earth tones, walnut-stained millwork and natural stone. Plentiful windows offer sweeping views of lavender and neighboring vineyards.

Amenities include an additional prep kitchen, an elevator and an outdoor brick oven. A secondary unit is a tranquil spot with the same luxury finishes.

For more information on Monte-Bellaria at 3518 Bloomfield Road in Sebastopol, contact listing agents Mallory Lambert Silipo, 707-478-5342, Pamela Ranella, 707-810-5066; Home Girls of Sonoma County, 130 Petaluma Ave., Suite 1-C, Sebastopol, 3518bloomfieldroad.com
